newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: JCI, Lonrho close to outline merger plan.
newsitem.headline: JCI, Lonrho close to outline merger plan.

text.p: South African mining house JCI Ltd and British conglomerate Lonrho Plc could finalise a broad-based merger agreement within 10 days, sources close to the companies said on Monday.
"A deal like this won't be finalised for some time, but soon, even within the next 10 days, there could be agreement on a broad base to go into the merger," one source told Reuters.
Such an agreement would open the door to due dilgence investigations into merger ratios and management structures.
Analysts said due diligence investigations could be launched soon but that getting a final green light to combine the two groups would take a lot longer.
"Agreement in principle is likely in a couple of weeks but the thrashing out of a final agreement is likely to take a very long time," said one analyst who asked not to be identified.
JCI's make-up differed a lot from sugar-to-mining-to-hotels group Lonrho and this could make shareholders on either side a little hesitant in giving the nod to a merger, analysts said.

"A broad-based agreement will enable them to do a due diligence but it doesn't give any indication of how they're going to merge. It could take quite a while," said Trevor Pearton, head of mining research at Societe Generale Frankel Pollak.
A 50/50 partnership between JCI and Lonrho was the most likely merger ratio, analysts said.
"No party must be seen to be losing, therefore a 50/50 arrangement is most likely," Pearton said.
London reports said last month, when merger talks were first announced, that Lonrho wanted a 60/40 split in its favour.
The two groups confirmed on May 19 that they were in talks on a possible merger which could create a company with market capitalisation of more than $3 billion.
JCI's new black management was unlikely to relinquish power so soon in favour of British management, analysts said.
Mzi Khumalo -- South Africa's first black "randlord" -- took the reins of JCI after black empowerment consortium African Mining Group, led by him, bought 34.9 percent of JCI last year.
"One of the critical issues is that Khumalo must be the key person or co-key person in the company, otherwise he hasn't achieved black empowerment," Pearton said.
Analysts said there were three possible management structure scenarios of which joint chairmanship between Khumalo and Lonrho's John Craven was the most likely.

Otherwise the merger could see shared boards with a single elected chairman, or Lonrho could take over the merged group. Newspaper reports on Sunday tipped Lonrho's South African head Terence Wilkinson as frontrunner for the post of JCI-Lonrho chief executive.

Analysts said rumours were circulating that certain JCI managers cold resign and that if this happened it could push the merger deal in Lonrho's favour. But they declined to elaborate further on the rumours.
A cat among the pigeons is giant Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd and its role in the proposed merger considering its involvement in the two groups concerned.

African Mining Group bought its 34.9 percent JCI stake from Anglo and Anglo retains a 5.5 percent stake in the JCI and has stakes in at least one of its gold mines. Anglo holds 27.5 percent of Lonrho but has been told by the European Commission to cut its stake to less than 10 percent in two years.
Anglo has made it clear it is interested in Lonrho's shareholding in Ghana's Ashanti Gold Fields Co Ltd.

"It's true that Anglo wants to get its hands on Ashanti. It could get Lonrho to buy back its 27 percent that Anglo has in exchange for Lonrho conceding its Ashanti interest. It would be neat because Lonrho could reduce the number of shares it has in issue and that way the JCI merger would be more equitable," said an analyst who asked not to be identified.

The local Business Times on Sunday proposed another alternative and that was Anglo selling its Lonrho stake to JCI in return for the Ashanti shares. It said that the Ghanaian government had been approached to back a deal with Anglo.
